Plan: Tomate, a Pomodoro time tracker for Omarchy

A small native app with one job: pick a project, run focus sessions and breaks with timings you choose, and get a calendar that shows exactly when the work happened. Everything is stored in one SQLite file on your machine.

1Background

Why this app, and what it borrows from apps you already like.

Beginner ramp (skip if you like)
  • Pomodoro: you work in fixed focus blocks (classically 25 min) separated by short breaks (5 min), and every few rounds (usually 4) you take a long break (15 min).
  • Clockify is a time tracker: you attach running time to a project, and later you look at a calendar or report to see where the hours went.
  • Session (macOS) puts the two together: a good-looking focus timer with categories and a timeline of past sessions.
  • Omarchy apps (Hype, Monologue, Omacut) are small C++ / Qt Quick binaries that follow your theme live, work well from the keyboard, and install as an Arch package so they show up in the launcher.

The search found plenty of Linux Pomodoro timers that look nice (GNOME Sessions, Tempus, Samaya), but none of them has projects or a history you can see on a calendar. The apps that do have those, like Super Productivity, are full task managers built on Electron. That leaves a gap for something simple: a Session-style timer whose every focus block also becomes a Clockify-style calendar entry.

Session: beautiful timer+ Clockify: projects + calendar+ Omarchy: theme, keyboard, launcher→ tomate
Scope, in one sentence

Projects, Pomodoro presets you can configure, a timer, and a calendar of past sessions. No tasks, kanban boards, teams, sync or invoicing.

2Intuition

Think of Tomate as a timer that keeps a diary. Each completed (or stopped) focus block becomes one row with a project, a start and an end. The calendar just draws those rows.

Why timestamps matter

The timer never counts seconds. It saves started_at and works out what’s left from the clock, so a laptop suspend, a crash or a restart can’t lose or inflate time. When the app reopens mid-session, it picks up where it was.

Mock-up with made-up data. In the real app the colours follow the active Omarchy theme, including dark ones like Tokyo Night.

Timer: the screen you leave open

The ring is the hero, as it is in Session. Above it are the project picker (press P for a fuzzy search) and an optional one-line intention that is saved as the session’s note and shows on the calendar block. Below the ring are three small preset chips: the project’s default is selected, and you can override it for one session. A slim bar at the bottom shows today’s total against your daily goal, coloured by project. The ring changes colour with the phase: accent while you focus, green during short breaks, purple during long breaks.

Change the times for just this session

Click the countdown (or press E) and the ring turns into small editors for focus, break and rounds. Type any minutes you like, for example 40 / 8 × 2, and press Enter. The new times apply to the current cycle only and the preset stays unchanged. The chip row shows a Custom 40/8 chip until the cycle ends. Press Ctrl+S in the editor if you want to keep it as a new preset.

Calendar: where the work happened

The week view is the default, as in Clockify: one column per day, one block per focus session, coloured by project, with a red “now” line. Click a block to change its project, times or note, or to delete it. Drag on an empty area to add time manually for work done away from the computer. The side panel shows the week’s totals per project. Day view is the same layout with one wide column. Month view is a heatmap with one square per day, where a deeper colour means more focus time:

Projects and presets

A project is just a name, a colour from the theme’s palette and a default preset. Archiving a project hides it from the picker but keeps its history on the calendar. A preset is the four numbers (focus, short break, long break, long break every N) plus whether breaks and the next focus start automatically. The small timeline under each preset card shows one full cycle to scale, so you can see how 50/10 compares with 25/5 at a glance.

4Data: local only

One SQLite file, three tables. No account, no server, no sync.

~/.local/share/tomate/
tomate.dbprojects, presets, sessions; the only thing to back up
~/.config/tomate/
settings.tomldaily goal, sounds, week starts on Monday

projects

What you trackname · colour · preset
id, name, colour (theme slot, so it changes with the theme), default preset, archived flag, created_at.

presets

How you workthe four numbers + automation
id, name, focus/short/long minutes, long break every N, auto-start breaks, auto-start focus. Ships with Classic, Deep and Sprint.

sessions

What happenedone row per focus block
id, project, started_at, ended_at, planned minutes, kind (focus or manual), completed or stopped early, note. Breaks are not stored. The running session is a row with no ended_at, which is how a restart resumes it.
Stopped early still counts

If you stop at minute 18 of 25, the row keeps 18 real minutes and is marked “stopped”. The calendar shows it with a dashed edge. Time you actually worked never disappears.

Your data stays usable

tomate export --csv --from 2026-11-01 writes the sessions out for a spreadsheet or invoice, and tomate report --week --json gives totals per project, which an agent can read too.

5Build phases

Five steps. Each one ends with something you can open and use.

Skeleton next

An empty Tomate window that looks like it belongs on Omarchy.

Scaffold the project the Omarchy way
C++ and Qt Quick, qmake6 + make, flat src/, bin/build, bin/test, bin/install, PKGBUILD, .desktop file and icon, in ~/Work/tomate.
Follow the theme live
Read the accent and palette from the current Omarchy theme, watch for theme switches, and read the corner radius from Hyprland.
Add the rail and four empty screens
Keys 1–4 switch screens, ? opens the shortcut overlay, Q quits.
Done when: it opens from Super+Space and changes colour when you switch themes

Timer later

A complete Pomodoro cycle with presets.

Build the timer state machine in C++
Idle → focus → short/long break → focus…, with pause, skip and stop. Remaining time is computed from timestamps, and unit tests cover the cycle and suspend/resume.
Draw the ring screen
Ring, phase label, round dots, preset chips, buttons, today bar, and the inline editor that sets custom times for one cycle (E).
Notify at each phase change
Desktop notification plus a short sound via Qt Multimedia, each with a toggle.
Done when: a 3-round Deep cycle runs on its own and survives a suspend

Projects + DB later

Every focus block lands in SQLite under a project.

Create the database and migrations
The three tables from section 4, versioned so future changes can migrate safely. Default presets are seeded on first run.
Build the Projects and Presets screens
Create, rename, recolour and archive projects; edit presets with the to-scale timeline.
Log sessions and resume after restart
Write the row when focus starts, close it when focus ends, and reopen a running session on launch.
Done when: kill the app mid-session, reopen it, and the countdown continues

Calendar later

See and fix where the time went.

Build the week view
Day columns, blocks coloured by project, now line, per-project totals.
Edit, delete and add blocks
Popover editor; drag on an empty area to add manual time; undo with Ctrl+Z.
Add Day and Month views
Day is one wide column; Month is the heatmap.
Done when: last week’s real sessions look right and can be corrected

Waybar + polish later

Use it all day without looking at the window.

Add the CLI commands
status --json, toggle, skip, report, export --csv, running headless.
Add the Waybar module, Hyprland bind and mini mode
Snippets to paste into your Waybar and Hyprland config (documented, not applied automatically) plus a floating mini window.
Package and install
bin/install → makepkg, README with a screenshot.
Done when: a full workday tracked from the bar, then reviewed on the calendar

7Quiz

Five quick questions to check the plan holds together.

1. You suspend the laptop at 20:00 left in a focus block and wake it 5 minutes later. What does Tomate show?

✅ B. The timer stores started_at and computes what’s left from the clock, so wall time is always correct. (Whether suspended minutes should count as work is a separate question, which idle detection could handle later.)

2. Where does the calendar get its blocks from?

✅ C. Each focus block writes one session row (project, start, end). The calendar only draws those rows, so editing a block means editing its row.

3. You stop a 25-minute focus block at minute 18. What ends up in the history?

✅ A. Real worked time is kept and flagged as “stopped”, and the calendar draws it with a dashed edge. Time is never invented, and time you worked is never lost.

4. How does the Waybar countdown get its value?

✅ B. A headless CLI command reports the running session (phase, time left, project) as JSON. That makes the database the single source of truth, so the bar, the window and the calendar always agree.

5. You archive the project “Old client”. What happens to last month’s blocks?

✅ C. Archiving is a flag, not a delete. History is never rewritten by tidying up your project list.
